statement: Open Problem 4.1 Construct a pair of algorithms Gen and Eval with the following properties. • Given integers n ≥ m ≥ t, Gen produces a (n, m, t)-covering design (Definition A.3) S1 , · · · , Sk (and also outputs some context to pass to Eval). That is, (S1 , · · · , Sk , context) ← Gen(n, m, t), (4.4) where S1 , · · · , Sk ⊆ [n] and ∀i ∈ [k] |Si | = m and ∀T ⊆ [n] |T | ≤ t =⇒ ∃i ∈ [k] T ⊆ Si . • The number of sets k should be not too large; ideally k ≤ C(n, m, t) · poly(n), where C(n, m, t) is the smallest possible k. • Given v ∈ [n] and I ⊆ [k], Eval indicates whether the collection [n] \ Si for i ∈ I has a hitting set of size ≤ v. That is, Eval(v, I, context) = true ⇐⇒ ∃T ⊆ [n] |T | ≤ v ∧ ∀i ∈ I T ∩ ([n] \ Si ) ̸= ∅. (4.5)
context: In the black-box setting the function f is indeed arbitrary. The input x is i.i.d., but from an arbitrary distribution. Crucially, the sets S1 , · · · , Sk are not arbitrary; our algorithm can choose them, subject only to the constraint that they form a covering design. This points to an avenue for making the algorithm computationally efficient – construct a covering design with additional structural properties that make the decision problem in Equation 4.3 easy. We formulate this precisely as an open problem: Open Problem 4.1 Construct a pair of algorithms Gen and Eval with the following properties. • Given integers n ≥ m ≥ t, Gen produces a (n, m, t)-covering design (Definition A.3) S1 , · · · , Sk (and also outputs some context to pass to Eval). That is, (S1 , · · · , Sk , context) ← Gen(n, m, t), (4.4) where S1 , · · · , Sk ⊆ [n] and ∀i ∈ [k] |Si | = m and ∀T ⊆ [n] |T | ≤ t =⇒ ∃i ∈ [k] T ⊆ Si . • The number of sets k should be not too large; ideally k ≤ C(n, m, t) · poly(n), where C(n, m, t) is the smallest possible k. • Given v ∈ [n] and I ⊆ [k], Eval indicates whether the collection [n] \ Si for i ∈ I has a hitting set of size ≤ v. That is, Eval(v, I, context) = true ⇐⇒ ∃T ⊆ [n] |T | ≤ v ∧ ∀i ∈ I T ∩ ([n] \ Si ) ̸= ∅. (4.5) • Both Gen and Eval should be computationally efficient for the parameter regime of interest. Ideally, their runtime should be polynomial in the parameter n and the covering size k. (Note that k ≥ C(n, m, t) may be exponential in n per Proposition A.4.) The algorithms Gen and Eval may be randomised; it suffices for the guarantees in Equations 4.4 and 4.5 to hold with high probability, although the dependence of k and the algorithms’ runtimes on the failure probability should be polylogarithmic. Tying the open problem back to our application: Algorithm 1 would first call Gen to produce the sets S1 , · · · , Sk (and context). Then it would evaluate f (x[n]\Si ) for each i ∈ [k]. Finally, it would run the shifted inverse mechanism (see Appendix B for details); this requires evaluating ℓ(x, y) for various values of y, which depends on f . Per Equations 4.3 and 4.5, ℓ(x, y) ≤ v ⇐⇒ Eval(v, I, context) = true, where I = {i ∈ [k] : f (x[n]\Si ) > y}. (4.6) Thus ℓ(x, y) can be evaluated by calling Eval and performing binary search on v ∈ {0, 1, 2, · · · , n}. Overall, to implement Theorem 2.5 the runtime of Algorithm 1 would be dominated by the runtime of one call to Gen, plus k calls to f , plus O(log(n) · log |Y|) calls to Eval.9
